rules.rule: The 2-hour rule: never leave cooked food or other perishables at room temperature for more than 2 hours, or 1 hour if it's above 90°F. This includes leftovers, doggie bags and takeout.
Keep the fridge at 40°F (4°C) or below and the freezer at 0°F (-18°C). Check both with an appliance thermometer.
Cool food quickly. Divide large batches into shallow containers (no more than about 2 inches deep), and never put a big pot of hot soup straight into the fridge.
Reheat leftovers and casseroles to 165°F, checked with a food thermometer.
Label and date everything. Put tape on the container with the date, use refrigerated leftovers within 3–4 days, and freeze what you won't eat in time.
Food held at 0°F stays safe indefinitely. Freezer times are for best quality (flavor and texture), not safety. Wrap food airtight to prevent freezer burn.
Thaw safely in the fridge, in cold water, or in the microwave, never on the counter. Cook food thawed in cold water or the microwave right away.
When in doubt, throw it out. Food can make you sick even when it looks, smells and tastes fine, and moldy food should be discarded.

rows.fridge: 3–4 days (Clemson lists up to 7 for plain rice)
rows.tips: Rice can carry Bacillus cereus spores, so spread it out to cool fast. Reheat with about 2 tbsp of water per cup until steaming.

rows.food: Cooked quinoa, millet and other whole grains
rows.freezer: Up to 6 months (handle like cooked rice)
rows.tips: Cool on a sheet pan and freeze in flat portion bags. Note: Clemson gives this time for rice; we apply it to other cooked grains.

rows.freezer: Freezes poorly (GF pasta softens); 1–2 months if you must
rows.tips: Undercook slightly, rinse, toss with a little oil, and store the pasta and sauce separately. Clemson gives no freezer time; ours is a quality estimate.

rows.food: Pizza dough or other unbaked yeast dough
rows.tips: Longer freezing weakens the yeast. Thaw overnight in the fridge.
Put parchment between tortillas before freezing. Corn tortillas dry out in the fridge, so warm them in a skillet. Times are NDSU's for homemade bread without preservatives.

rows.freezer: 4 months (6 months covered in broth or gravy)
rows.tips: Shred or slice before freezing. Reheat to 165°F.

rows.food: Cooked ground meat and meat dishes (taco meat, meatballs, chili meat)
rows.tips: Cool in shallow containers. Freeze it flat in bags so it thaws quickly.

rows.food: Cooked beef or pork roast, shredded beef, pulled pork
rows.tips: Cut large roasts into smaller pieces to chill. Freeze with some of the cooking juices to prevent dryness.
Reheat gently, or flake it cold into salads.
Freeze them in their cooking liquid in about 2-cup (one-can) portions. UMN lists this time for vegetable soups and stews; we apply it to cooked beans.
Use a clean spoon each time and keep it covered with a thin layer of olive oil. Time is CSU's for homemade dips.
Change the storage water every day or two. Frozen tofu turns chewier, which works well in stir-fries.
Divide a big pot into shallow containers to cool. Bring to a boil when reheating.

rows.food: Homemade meat broth, stock or bone broth, and gravy
rows.tips: Use or freeze it fast. Freeze in 1-cup portions or ice-cube trays, and skim the fat after chilling.
Freeze in jars with headspace, or in flat bags. Time is UMN's for vegetable soups.

rows.food: Tomato sauce, marinara, pizza sauce (homemade or opened jar)
rows.freezer: Freezes well; about 3 months for best quality
rows.tips: Move opened canned tomato products into glass or plastic; don't store them in the can. NDSU gives no freezer time; ours is a quality estimate.

rows.food: Pesto (basil, seed-based) and herb or garlic-in-oil sauces
rows.tips: Garlic and herbs in oil can support botulism, so keep these cold and freeze them in ice-cube trays.

rows.fridge: About 1 week; up to 4 days if made with fresh garlic or herbs in oil
rows.tips: Oil firms up in the fridge, so let it sit for 5 minutes and shake. Garlic powder keeps longer than fresh garlic.

rows.food: Homemade egg-free mayo (aquafaba) and creamy dressings
rows.tips: Homemade versions aren't pasteurized or commercially acidified like store mayo, so keep them cold and use clean utensils. Time is CSU's for homemade dips.
Refrigerate cut fruit promptly. For longer storage, tray-freeze the pieces and then bag them.
Freeze in moisture- and vapor-proof bags or jars and blend straight from frozen.

rows.food: Cut raw vegetables and salad greens
rows.tips: Store them in moisture-resistant bags or containers with a paper towel. Celery, lettuce and cucumbers don't freeze well.

rows.freezer: Texture suffers; freeze only for soups and purées
rows.tips: Reheat on a hot sheet pan to bring back some crispness.

rows.fridge: Not recommended: the fridge makes bread stale faster
rows.tips: GF bread stales fast, so slice it before freezing and toast slices straight from frozen.

rows.fridge: Only if not eaten in 3–4 days
rows.tips: Cool completely, then wrap individually before freezing.
Freeze cookie dough balls to bake fresh. Baked cookies thaw in minutes.
Freeze unfrosted layers wrapped twice. Refrigerate cakes with whipped or creamy fillings.
Cool completely before wrapping. Re-crisp in a 350°F oven.
Freeze them in a single layer, then bag them. Reheat in the toaster or oven.
Re-whip briefly before serving. Time is CSU's for whipped topping prepared from a mix (some recipes claim longer).

rows.food: Opened canned coconut milk or coconut cream
rows.tips: Move it out of the can into a covered jar. Frozen coconut milk separates, so use it for cooking. Time is CSU's for opened evaporated milk.

rows.food: Opened plant milk (soy, oat, coconut carton)
rows.fridge: Up to 1 week after opening (or by the label)
rows.tips: Freezing changes the texture, so use thawed milk for cooking and baking. Times are CSU's for soy milk.

rows.food: Flax eggs, chia eggs and whipped aquafaba
rows.fridge: Best made fresh (use the same day)
rows.tips: No official chart covers these, so make them fresh just before using. Keep ground flaxseed itself in the fridge.
Move it into microwave-safe dishes; don't reheat in foam or carry-out containers. Reheat until steaming (165°F).
Cool in shallow pans. Reheat covered to 165°F in the center.
